Execution evidence · CycloneDX 1.6

A signed run,
in a standard parts list.

An ingredients label, with a signed receipt stapled in. See the files that ran, the room they ran in, and what came back.

A bill of materials (BOM) is a parts list for software. CycloneDX is the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s standard format for that list. This example puts one run into the list. The image’s own ingredients label is linked separately when supplied.

Plimsoll runs code in a sandbox, like a locked room. A digest is a fingerprint of some bytes, made here with the SHA-256 hash algorithm. Change one letter and the fingerprint changes. The request is the files and commands sent into the room. The result is what came back.

The daemon, a long-running server named plimsolld, returns a run record: the fingerprints, image, room’s isolation tier and times. A harness, a separate checking program, checks that record and seals it. We call that sealed record the receipt. The seal is a tamper strip, like the one on a medicine bottle.

The signed wrapper is a Dead Simple Signing Envelope (DSSE). Inside it, an in-toto statement is a standard way to write a claim. CycloneDX Attestations (CDXA) attach the receipt as evidence for the list’s three claims: code, image and isolation.

This converter needs a selected OCI manifest identity, the exact fingerprint of one container image for one platform. Today that means docker on the containerd image store. Other providers’ runs are refused when that identity is missing.

The record is signed. The BOM is unsigned. The seal lets you spot changed evidence. It does not independently measure the room’s walls. The daemon supplies those facts. A key included with the receipt shows which key checks the seal; you still need an independently trusted key to know the signer.

The evidence path

From execution to a checkable file

1. RequestThe program's files, commands, minimum isolation tier and timeout.
2. RecordThe daemon's statement of what was sent, returned and used to run it.
3. BundleThe harness checks fingerprints, then signs records and entry links.
4. BOMThe emitter checks the bundle. A reviewer can rebuild the mapping from it.
One network attempt, two settings

The failure is preserved with its evidence

The program attempts to fetch https://example.com/. Its own five-second timer bounds the demonstration, so it cannot wait indefinitely. The sandboxed attempt failed; the outside transcript reports success.

Inside plimsoll

Signed exchange

node egress.js
Exit 3, duration 5228 milliseconds.

egress: refused: TimeoutError

The word “refused” comes from the guest program. Its fetch timer expired; the sandbox timeout flag is false. The timeout is consistent with the provider's reported network configuration, but does not independently establish its cause.

Outside plimsoll

Unsigned transcript
# record: af0fa2597b817e6bff801ac2c6d3fcef1cb51661c9cce1a5e4a1bd1c29687927
# step: node egress.js
# The same egress attempt outside plimsoll
#
# Command, run on the developer machine on 2026-10-13 with the node on PATH (v26.3.1),
# default network, no sandbox, no record of any kind:
#
#   node egress.js
#
# Output and exit code, pasted by hand (there is no signed record to cite):

egress: reached example.com, status 200
exit code: 0

The same file reached the internet outside the room, while nobody wrote a signed receipt. This text was pasted by hand. There is nothing sealed for the converter to staple into a BOM. The two settings also used different runtimes; this comparison does not establish why the inside attempt failed.

One failed request is an observed result, not a universal proof that every network path is blocked. The full sandbox boundary still rests on the daemon and its provider checks.

The signed source exchange

The run

Outcome: completedStated tier: kernel

The completed outcome means the runner returned a normal result; a step with a nonzero exit code still failed. “Kernel” is the daemon's reported isolation tier, backed by provider configuration and startup checks, never runtime attestation.

Open Container Initiative (OCI) is the container image format. The manifest digest identifies the selected image for one platform, such as Linux on a standard PC processor (linux/amd64). A display name never supplies that identity.

The program's files

reconcile.js

SHA-256: c2de8205ca1e811fba188b71b051e25644f88b8190351372ab3ed4a842231456

// reconcile.js: match payments to invoices by invoice id and report what is
// unpaid, overpaid or matched. Amounts are integer cents.
function reconcile(invoices, payments) {
  const paid = new Map();
  for (const p of payments) paid.set(p.invoice, (paid.get(p.invoice) || 0) + p.cents);
  const matched = [], unpaid = [], overpaid = [];
  for (const inv of invoices) {
    const got = paid.get(inv.id) || 0;
    if (got === inv.cents) matched.push(inv.id);
    else if (got < inv.cents) unpaid.push({ id: inv.id, owed: inv.cents - got });
    else overpaid.push({ id: inv.id, excess: got - inv.cents });
  }
  return { matched, unpaid, overpaid };
}
module.exports = { reconcile };
reconcile.test.js

SHA-256: ce76efdec6de19969e12f5ca27b273396ca274dfa330df36811f78354c659c97

const assert = require("node:assert/strict");
const { reconcile } = require("./reconcile.js");
const invoices = [
  { id: "INV-1001", cents: 12500 },
  { id: "INV-1002", cents: 8000 },
  { id: "INV-1003", cents: 4200 },
];
const payments = [
  { invoice: "INV-1001", cents: 12500 },
  { invoice: "INV-1002", cents: 5000 },
  { invoice: "INV-1003", cents: 4200 },
  { invoice: "INV-1003", cents: 300 },
];
const r = reconcile(invoices, payments);
assert.deepEqual(r.matched, ["INV-1001"]);
assert.deepEqual(r.unpaid, [{ id: "INV-1002", owed: 3000 }]);
assert.deepEqual(r.overpaid, [{ id: "INV-1003", excess: 300 }]);
console.log("reconcile: 3 assertions passed");

The commands and recorded results

Standard output (stdout) is printed output; standard error (stderr) is the separate diagnostic channel. Exit code 0 means the command reported success. A nonzero code means it reported failure.

Try the receipt here

The seal is a tamper strip, like the one on a medicine bottle. Check it, then change a copy and watch the seal fail. Your browser uses only the bytes inside this page.

Checking whether this browser can verify the seal.

    This checks one receipt and its JSON fields. The emitter's Go checker also verifies the complete bundle and proves that the JSON copy matches the stored protobuf messages. An attached public key proves consistency under that key; it does not tell you who owns it.

    Checks actually run by the emitter

    These receipts come from checking the generated BOM and three separately altered copies. The original source files are unchanged.

    PASS: CycloneDX 1.6 schema (vendored, offline).
PASS: DSSE envelope signature and run-record digest.
PASS: bundle signatures, checkpoint links, stored request and result digests.
PASS: exchange.json equals the bundle's protobuf messages and reproduces their digests.
PASS: file-set digest recomputed from file components and bound to the signed request.
PASS: every mapped field and claim matches the verified exchange.
PASS: attached key matches independently trusted key.
LIMIT: names, page URL and assessor label are unsigned presentation; runtime assertions remain the daemon's statements.
PASS: image SBOM hash, manifest identity and BOM-Link match the local evidence file.
PASS: altered envelope refused: envelope: attest: no valid signature from this key
PASS: altered file hash refused: file-set digest differs from program hash
PASS: altered claim digest refused: BOM differs from the verified exchange: file contents, digests, claims or another mapped field was changed

    reconcile.js

    SHA-256: c2de8205ca1e811fba188b71b051e25644f88b8190351372ab3ed4a842231456

    // reconcile.js: match payments to invoices by invoice id and report what is
// unpaid, overpaid or matched. Amounts are integer cents.
function reconcile(invoices, payments) {
  const paid = new Map();
  for (const p of payments) paid.set(p.invoice, (paid.get(p.invoice) || 0) + p.cents);
  const matched = [], unpaid = [], overpaid = [];
  for (const inv of invoices) {
    const got = paid.get(inv.id) || 0;
    if (got === inv.cents) matched.push(inv.id);
    else if (got < inv.cents) unpaid.push({ id: inv.id, owed: inv.cents - got });
    else overpaid.push({ id: inv.id, excess: got - inv.cents });
  }
  return { matched, unpaid, overpaid };
}
module.exports = { reconcile };
    reconcile.test.js

    SHA-256: ce76efdec6de19969e12f5ca27b273396ca274dfa330df36811f78354c659c97

    const assert = require("node:assert/strict");
const { reconcile } = require("./reconcile.js");
const invoices = [
  { id: "INV-1001", cents: 12500 },
  { id: "INV-1002", cents: 8000 },
  { id: "INV-1003", cents: 4200 },
];
const payments = [
  { invoice: "INV-1001", cents: 12500 },
  { invoice: "INV-1002", cents: 5000 },
  { invoice: "INV-1003", cents: 4200 },
  { invoice: "INV-1003", cents: 300 },
];
const r = reconcile(invoices, payments);
assert.deepEqual(r.matched, ["INV-1001"]);
assert.deepEqual(r.unpaid, [{ id: "INV-1002", owed: 3000 }]);
assert.deepEqual(r.overpaid, [{ id: "INV-1003", excess: 300 }]);
console.log("reconcile: 3 assertions passed");

    // egress.js: one benign network attempt, so the record shows what the boundary
// did with it. Outside plimsoll this reaches example.com; inside, with no grant,
// there is no network, and the exit code says so.
fetch("https://example.com/", { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })
  .then((r) => { console.log("egress: reached example.com, status", r.status); process.exit(0); })
  .catch((e) => { console.error("egress: refused:", (e.cause && e.cause.code) || e.name); process.exit(3); });

      The image’s ingredients label

      The run’s image has a known ingredients list: 694 components, generated by syft 1.54.1 at 2026-10-13T16:52:12-07:00. A platform that already adds vulnerability information to that list can show it beside the run. This page makes no claim that those lookups have happened.

      The label’s root version and the receipt’s selected image fingerprint are the same string: sha256:1c6cbab4a47d34da471ab4ab970709cbba18e2a3445fde884b5d90ec2c4c5b25. The run’s image component links to the label by its URL and file fingerprint, and by BOM-Link, a reference to one component inside another bill of materials.

      INTERNAL · image ingredients JSON → · EXTERNAL · official BOM-Link docs ↗

      How the pinned image label was made

      The scanner read the image’s OCI layout, the original container image files, rather than a rewritten manifest returned by a legacy image interface. That keeps the join exact. The label is CycloneDX 1.7; its random serial number is kept as evidence and is never regenerated by the gate.

      docker image save plimsoll/sandbox:latest | tar -xf - -C tmp/image-layout/oci
tmp/syft-dl/syft oci-dir:tmp/image-layout/oci --platform linux/amd64 \
  --source-name plimsoll/sandbox -o cyclonedx-json=tmp/sbom-poc/image.cdx.json

      The syft 1.54.1 release binary was checked against its release checksum file. The published file fingerprint is 67f4c52093e4e364b86fb1d7db9cbda8572d25afc906e4cac6ec738a57dd0292.

      The program’s own fingerprint

      Think of a file-set fingerprint as a fingerprint of the whole folder. The exact recipe follows. The file-set digest separates the program from its execution settings. Sort files by path. For each file, concatenate the 32 raw bytes of SHA-256(path) followed by the 32 raw bytes of SHA-256(content). SHA-256 of that entire concatenation is the file-set digest.

      The request fingerprint uses plimsoll.run-request.v2 for protocol 2 and later, and plimsoll.run-request.v1 for protocol 1. The protocol is the request format revision. The result uses plimsoll.run-result.v1 and these records use plimsoll.run-record.v2. Each value is its length as an unsigned 64-bit big-endian integer followed by its bytes. Fields are encoded as name then value, in the reference order. Integers are decimal text, booleans are true or false, strings are UTF-8, and printed output keeps its raw bytes. The request fingerprint also covers the protocol version (the request-format revision), minimum isolation tier, timeout and software rule, so it is a different identity. The file-set fingerprint remains bound to the signed request because the checker compares the file list with the request stored in the verified bundle.

      How thick are the walls?

      An isolation tier is the kind of boundary around the code. Think of process as a cubicle, container as a room with a lock, kernel as a room with its own plumbing, and vm as a separate building, a virtual machine. These are analogies, not safety ratings.

      These runs asked for kernel. The daemon reported that tier after checking gVisor, a user-space kernel between the program and the host. The record preserves that report. It is configuration and provider evidence plus startup checks, never hardware attestation, an independent measurement from the machine itself.

      The trust boundary

      What the checks establish

      They establish that the evidence verifies under its key, that the bundle is complete through its last checkpoint (a signed entry-count statement), and that each BOM field derived from the exchange agrees with it. -trusted-pub additionally requires the attached key to match a key obtained independently.

      What remains outside that check

      The attached run record is signed; this BOM is unsigned. Agent authorship is supplied example context, not a record fact, and the execution layer cannot identify the model. No host-API grant was requested. Network isolation is provider configuration, not a separately signed runtime measurement. The run's times are the daemon's own unwitnessed clock. An attached key alone establishes consistency, not signer identity; use an independently trusted key. Display names and the assessor label are unsigned presentation. This is run evidence, not an inventory of the image's installed packages.

      A score of 1 in conformance or confidence means a deterministic signature and mapping check passed. It does not mean perfect security, independent runtime assurance or a measured probability. Names, the page URL and assessor labels can be changed without re-signing evidence.

      This run’s BOM is a receipt, not a package scan. A software bill of materials (SBOM) for the image is a separate ingredients label, linked when supplied. Neither label shows that vulnerability lookups have been done. Schema validity does not establish platform ingestion or rendering. A viewer supporting these fields can display components, hashes and references; support for declarations must be tested per platform. No platform round trip has been tested here.

      Each list includes the whole bundle, the file holding the sealed records and their stored messages. That makes this small example easy to check on its own. Large batches would repeat too much data. Input is capped at 32 MiB to fit the request and result budgets plus attachment encoding. A larger service should share the bundle by fingerprint and attach each selected entry with an equally strong check.

      Reproduce and review

      From a checkout of plimsoll, run these commands. Generation reuses the evidence and starts no sandbox. Tests use pinned schemas without network access after Go dependencies are available.

      cd examples/sbom
go run .
go run . -check ../../docs/examples/sbom/run-c7e245a369dd.cdx.json -trusted-pub ../../docs/examples/sbom/harness.pub
go run . -check ../../docs/examples/sbom/run-af0fa2597b81.cdx.json -trusted-pub ../../docs/examples/sbom/harness.pub
cd ../..
make sbom-suite

      Successful checks print PASS. Changed evidence or a mapped field makes -check exit nonzero. Obtain the trusted key independently when reviewing another publisher's file; the copy next to this example is an illustrative pin.
